MUHAMMADIYAH.OR.ID, YOGYAKARTA – Anggota Dewan Perwakilan Daerah Republik Indonesia (DPD RI), Ahmad Syauqi Soeratno, memaparkan gagasan tentang arah pengembangan dakwah ekonomi Muhammadiyah dalam diskusi bersama Ketua Pimpinan Pusat Muhammadiyah, Anwar Abbas, yang disiarkan melalui TvMu Channel.

Dalam diskusi tersebut, Syauqi mengangkat hasil penelitian disertasinya yang memperkenalkan konsep Socio-Religiopreneurship. Gagasan ini kemudian dikaitkan dengan posisi Muhammadiyah sebagai Epistemic Community atau komunitas epistemik yang memiliki peran strategis dalam membangun pengetahuan dan merespons berbagai tantangan global.

Pertama, Syauqi menjelaskan bahwa konsep Socio-Religiopreneurship menawarkan pendekatan kewirausahaan yang tidak hanya berorientasi pada keuntungan ekonomi, tetapi juga berlandaskan nilai-nilai agama dan kemaslahatan sosial.

Berbeda dengan konsep bisnis global yang mengenal prinsip 3P (Profit, People, Planet), Syauqi menawarkan penambahan dimensi ketuhanan sebagai landasan dalam menjalankan aktivitas ekonomi. Dengan demikian, keberhasilan usaha tidak semata-mata diukur melalui keuntungan materi, tetapi juga manfaat sosial dan keberkahan yang dihasilkan.

“Socio-religiopreneurship itu satu konsepsi yang membawa cara berpikir kita, cara bertindak kita, cara bercakap kita mengenai entrepreneurship yang berbasis nilai agama dan sosial, dan memberi manfaat sosial,” jelas Syauqi yang juga merupakan Wakil Ketua Majelis Ekonomi dan Bisnis Pimpinan Pusat Muhammadiyah dalam siaran Jumat (20/11).

Menurutnya, prinsip tersebut sejatinya bukan sesuatu yang asing bagi Muhammadiyah. Selama lebih dari satu abad, Persyarikatan telah membuktikan bagaimana aktivitas ekonomi dan kewirausahaan dapat berjalan beriringan dengan misi dakwah serta pelayanan sosial.

Hal itu tercermin melalui keberadaan ratusan Perguruan Tinggi Muhammadiyah dan ‘Aisyiyah (PTMA), rumah sakit, ribuan sekolah, panti asuhan, hingga masjid yang tersebar di berbagai wilayah Indonesia. Berbagai amal usaha tersebut tidak hanya menjadi instrumen pengembangan organisasi, tetapi juga menghadirkan manfaat nyata bagi masyarakat.

Menariknya, dalam konsep Socio-Religiopreneurship, Syauqi juga menawarkan perspektif berbeda dalam memandang risiko (risk). Risiko tidak hanya dihitung berdasarkan potensi kerugian finansial, tetapi juga mempertimbangkan dimensi ukhrawi.

Artinya, aktivitas bisnis yang berpotensi menimbulkan risiko terhadap nilai-nilai agama dan tanggung jawab akhirat perlu dikaji secara mendalam. Dengan begitu, orientasi keuntungan tidak mengabaikan prinsip etika, kemaslahatan, dan keberkahan.

Poin kedua yang disampaikan Syauqi adalah pentingnya memahami Muhammadiyah sebagai Epistemic Community. Sebagai gerakan Islam dan tajdid, Muhammadiyah tidak hanya bergerak dalam bidang dakwah dan amal usaha, tetapi juga memiliki tradisi keilmuan yang menjadi fondasi dalam melahirkan gagasan dan perubahan sosial.

Menurut Syauqi, pengetahuan (knowledge) yang dibangun dan dikembangkan secara kolektif dapat melahirkan gagasan yang kemudian menjadi kontribusi nyata bagi bangsa dan masyarakat.

“Dan ketika knowledge itu bertemu menghasilkan satu gagasan. Gagasan itu menjadi bagian dari kontribusi komunitas ini kepada bangsa, kepada masyarakat,” katanya.

Berangkat dari karakter Muhammadiyah sebagai gerakan Islam, tajdid, serta gerakan ilmu dan amal, Syauqi mendorong kader Persyarikatan untuk memperkuat kiprah dakwah di sektor ekonomi. Upaya tersebut penting agar Muhammadiyah mampu mengambil peran dalam menghadapi persaingan ideologi sekaligus menjawab tantangan global yang semakin kompleks.

Dalam konteks tersebut, pembentukan mental kewirausahaan (entrepreneurial mindset) menjadi salah satu agenda penting. Syauqi menilai perlu adanya pergeseran orientasi dan mentalitas warga Persyarikatan, dari yang cenderung berorientasi sebagai pekerja (employee mindset) menuju karakter yang lebih mandiri, kreatif, dan berani membangun usaha (entrepreneurial mindset).

“Sejak zaman Kiai Dahlan, Kiai Sujak, Mbah Badawi, kalau dulu entrepreneurship ini sangat kuat. Sekarang ini lebih banyak karakter yang muncul dari warga Persyarikatan itu mereka yang masih bermental employee, bukan mental entrepreneur,” ujarnya.

Ketiga, sebagai langkah konkret untuk menghadapi persaingan ekonomi global, Syauqi mendorong Muhammadiyah membangun ekosistem ekonomi tertutup melalui konsep jamaah ekonomi. Dengan potensi pasar yang besar dari jutaan warga dan jaringan Persyarikatan, Muhammadiyah dinilai memiliki modal sosial dan ekonomi untuk membangun rantai nilai usaha yang terintegrasi.

Ekosistem tersebut perlu dikembangkan dari hulu hingga hilir, mulai dari proses produksi, distribusi, hingga konsumsi. Dengan demikian, potensi ekonomi warga Muhammadiyah tidak berjalan secara terpisah, tetapi dapat saling terhubung dan memperkuat satu sama lain.

“Syaratnya ada tiga. Pertama membangun Jamaah Ekonomi Persyarikatan, kedua harus terus belajar ilmu baru karena berilmu itu penting, dan yang ketiga melakukan konsolidasi gagasan terutama dari sisi finance, cash management yang akan menjadi energi bagi pengembangan ekonomi Persyarikatan,” pungkasnya. The new NVIDIA RTX Spark N1X can run Fallout 4 at 4K, but Elden Ring falls short of 60 fps at 1440p even on medium settings. This 140W desktop chip is aimed at AI work, yet its ARM CPU and Blackwell graphics also let you play games on a compact Windows workstation. Shared memory and Windows translation bring trade-offs, while DLSS and frame generation can improve results in some games. Find out what ETA Prime reports about gaming performance and how those trade-offs affect the games you play.

The New RTX Spark N1X workstation has 20 ARM cores, 6,144 CUDA cores, 128GB of unified memory and a 140W desktop TDP. Its approximately 300GB/s memory bandwidth is lower than the RTX 5070’s 672GB/s, and Prism translation adds overhead. The N1X scored around 14,086 in 3DMark Time Spy, ahead of RTX 5070 and RTX 5060 laptop averages. Gaming results varied: Fallout 4 held 60 fps at 4K ultra, while Elden Ring fell short of 60 fps at 1440p medium. Gears of War: E-Day averaged 46 fps without frame generation and 79 fps with it, using ultra settings and DLSS quality.

The RTX Spark N1X can run games on the MSI Edge Mesa NAI Plus, a small-form-factor workstation aimed more at AI work than gaming. The chip combines an ARM CPU and NVIDIA Blackwell graphics, with unified memory shared between the CPU and GPU rather than separate pools of system and graphics memory. It runs Windows with help from Microsoft’s Prism translation layer.

The desktop chip has more power headroom than the 20-core N1X laptops seen so far, allowing higher CPU and GPU clocks, but its memory bandwidth is lower than that of an RTX 5060 or RTX 5070. The workstation’s main specifications are:

In the tested system, memory was split evenly, with 64GB for Windows and 64GB for the GPU. In FurMark, the GPU drew close to 115 watts, while the CPU has been observed drawing from 51 to 68 watts. N1X laptops seen so far have generally reached around 85 watts, with some boosting to around 90 watts.

At 672GB per second, the RTX 5070 has higher memory bandwidth, while the N1X also has overhead from Prism translation. Extra power headroom should give the desktop variant much better performance than the laptop version, though that remains an expectation.

In synthetic benchmarks, the N1X scored ahead of RTX 5070 and RTX 5060 laptop averages, although those scores do not tell the whole story of game performance. At 140W, it scored around 14,086 in 3DMark Time Spy and 3,453 in 3DMark Steel Nomad.

Driver updates and further Prism work may improve performance, but the game results below show what the workstation delivered with its current software.

The workstation handled the esports games tested without frame generation, although Marvel Rivals was weaker than the other two results. Fortnite and Marvel Rivals used DLSS on its quality setting, and DLSS is likely to be useful for many of the games tested at 1440p.

The latest Fallout 4 update ran at a continuous 60 fps at 4K ultra, making older games a good fit for higher-resolution play. Left 4 Dead and Half-Life can also run with settings maxed out at 4K, while Street Fighter 5 and Injustice are expected to perform well at 4K ultra.

Elden Ring struggled to reach 60 fps at 1440p high, and reducing the settings to medium still left it short of that mark. At 1080p, it reached 60 fps on high settings and around 51 fps with settings maxed out.

Mortal Kombat 1 averaged around 51 fps at very high settings without DLSS. Dropping to high at 1440p, still without DLSS, produced a decent result, although ETA Prime notes that the game felt odd for a reason that was difficult to pinpoint.

DLSS made a difference in demanding titles, though the benefit varied by game. Ghost of Tsushima remained fully playable at 1440p ultra without DLSS or other scaling. Spider-Man 2 performed poorly without DLSS, but ran better than expected at 1440p high with DLSS quality and NVIDIA’s RTX Spark Game Ready driver.

Japanese Drift Master ran at 1440p ultra with DLSS set to balanced, while turning DLSS off at 1440p sent it into the low 40s fps. Hogwarts Legacy used DLSS frame generation at 1440p ultra, without multi-frame generation, which is also available on the chip.

Gears of War: E-Day gave the clearest frame-generation comparison: its built-in benchmark averaged 46 fps without frame generation and 79 fps with it, using the ultra preset and DLSS quality in both runs.

ETA Prime sees the MSI Edge Mesa NAI Plus as an AI workstation that handles its main job well while also letting you play games. It was not designed specifically for gaming, and results vary for players who prefer to avoid frame generation. Elden Ring reached 60 fps at 1080p high but fell short at 1440p, even on medium settings.

Samsung is preparing to make a significant impact on the smartphone market with the highly anticipated Galaxy S27 Ultra. This flagship device is rumored to feature a reimagined camera layout and potentially innovative display technology. If these rumors prove accurate, the S27 Ultra could represent a pivotal moment in Samsung’s design evolution, especially as it competes with Apple’s rumored bezel-less iPhone 20. The Galaxy S27 Ultra is poised to showcase Samsung’s commitment to innovation while addressing the growing demand for innovative features and aesthetics.

TL;DR Key Takeaways : Horizontal Camera Bar Shift: Leaks point to a wide camera plateau with individual lens cutouts, a 5x zoom lens, and a relocated LED flash replacing the laser autofocus sensor. Shared S27 Pro Look: The S27 Ultra and Galaxy S27 Pro are tipped to share a unified rear design language while keeping distinct camera and screen specs. Ultra-Thin Bezels & Quad-Curve Debate: Reports highlight ~1mm borders and ongoing speculation around quad-curved panels, with roughly 50/50 odds on how far Samsung pushes the curve on the Ultra. Software-Driven Focusing: Dropping dedicated laser autofocus puts greater weight on computational imaging and AI autofocus tuning to keep lock-on speed sharp.

The Galaxy S27 Ultra is expected to introduce a fresh approach to camera design, moving away from the traditional camera layout seen in previous models. Instead, Samsung appears to be adopting individual circular cutouts across a wider camera plateau, creating a cleaner and more modern aesthetic. This new layout includes a dedicated 5x zoom camera and a repositioned LED flash alongside the camera array, replacing the laser autofocus sensor used in earlier iterations.

The removal of the laser autofocus sensor raises questions about its potential impact on low-light and close-up focusing speed. However, Samsung may be relying on advancements in software-based focusing technologies and updated sensor processing to maintain or even enhance the camera’s capabilities. This design decision reflects Samsung’s broader strategy of balancing innovation with practicality, making sure that new features are both functional and visually appealing.

Interestingly, the Galaxy S27 Ultra is expected to share its overall rear design language with the Galaxy S27 Pro. This consistency across models could streamline production processes while maintaining a cohesive aesthetic across Samsung’s high-end lineup. By unifying the design, Samsung aims to create a recognizable and premium identity for its flagship devices.

One of the most exciting rumors surrounding the Galaxy S27 Ultra is its potential adoption of a nearly bezel-less display. Reports suggest that the device could feature an edge-to-edge screen with bezels as thin as 1mm, pushing the boundaries of screen-to-body ratios and delivering an immersive viewing experience. This design would cater to users seeking maximum screen real estate without compromising the device’s overall size.

There is also speculation about a quad-curved display that wraps around all four edges of the device, offering a futuristic and seamless look. However, this ambitious design may not debut on the S27 Ultra. Industry insiders suggest that extreme curved-edge designs could be reserved for a specialized or alternative model, such as a rumored Edge variant. This cautious approach likely stems from the technical challenges associated with implementing such a design, including concerns about durability, usability and manufacturing complexity.

While the bezel-less concept is undeniably appealing, it also presents challenges. Making sure the structural integrity of a device with such thin bezels requires innovative engineering solutions. Additionally, optimizing touch sensitivity and minimizing accidental touches on curved edges are critical factors that Samsung must address to deliver a practical and user-friendly experience.

The idea of a bezel-less display is undoubtedly intriguing, but its implementation is far from guaranteed. Experts estimate a 50% likelihood that an extreme bezel-less or quad-curved treatment will appear on the Galaxy S27 Ultra, citing the technical hurdles involved in mass production. These challenges include maintaining the device’s structural durability, preventing screen glare and making sure accurate touch responses.

Curved displays, while visually striking, have sparked mixed reactions among users. Some appreciate their sleek and modern appearance, while others find them less practical due to issues like accidental touches and reduced usability. Samsung will need to carefully balance aesthetics with functionality to ensure the design appeals to a wide range of consumers.

Additionally, the shift away from a laser autofocus sensor introduces another layer of uncertainty. While software advancements may compensate for the change, the real-world impact on camera performance remains to be seen. Samsung’s ability to address these challenges will play a crucial role in determining the success of the Galaxy S27 Ultra.

Samsung’s design innovations often reflect broader industry trends, particularly those set by its primary competitor, Apple. With Apple’s iPhone 20 rumored to feature a bezel-less, quad-curved display for its 20th anniversary, Samsung’s developments may be a strategic move to stay competitive. This rivalry has historically driven rapid advancements in smartphone technology, resulting in innovative features that benefit consumers.

The push for minimal bezel designs aligns with a growing industry focus on immersive displays. As smartphones become increasingly central to daily life, manufacturers are prioritizing designs that maximize screen real estate without sacrificing usability. Samsung’s efforts to innovate in this area highlight its commitment to meeting consumer demands while staying ahead of the competition.

Moreover, the Galaxy S27 Ultra’s design choices reflect a broader trend toward creating devices that balance form and function. By addressing both aesthetic and practical considerations, Samsung aims to deliver a product that appeals to a diverse audience, from tech enthusiasts to everyday users.

If you’re thinking about purchasing the Galaxy S27 Ultra, it’s important to evaluate how its rumored features align with your needs and preferences.

Ultimately, your decision will depend on your priorities. Whether you value innovative design, everyday functionality, or a balance of both, the Galaxy S27 Ultra promises to deliver a compelling combination of features and performance.

The Samsung Galaxy S27 Ultra represents a bold step forward in smartphone design, showcasing the company’s dedication to innovation and its ability to adapt to evolving market trends. With its updated camera layout and potential bezel-less display, the device highlights Samsung’s commitment to pushing technological boundaries while addressing consumer demands.

As competition with Apple intensifies, the Galaxy S27 Ultra could play a pivotal role in shaping the future of smartphone design. Whether you prioritize aesthetics, functionality, or a mix of both, this flagship device offers a glimpse into the possibilities of next-generation technology. For those seeking a smartphone that combines innovative features with a refined design, the Galaxy S27 Ultra is a product worth considering.

Apple has not announced an iPhone 20 Pro or confirmed any camera sensor changes for late 2027, yet fresh supply-chain chatter suggests Apple is looking beyond raw megapixel counts toward silicon-level imaging upgrades. According to Weibo tipster Ice Universe, the rumored 20th-anniversary flagship could pair a new main camera sensor with a 17-nanometer logic process—adding another layer to earlier reports around three-layer stacked sensors and LOFIC dynamic range technology. The video below from Demon’s Tech breaks down the latest reports.

17nm Sensor Logic Circuitry: Rumors point to a 17-nanometer manufacturing process for the main camera sensor’s logic/signal-processing layer to boost speed and power efficiency. Three-Layer Stacked & LOFIC Chatter: Separate supply-chain reports have linked Apple to three-layer stacked sensor development and LOFIC wide-dynamic-range tech, though links between those rumors remain unconfirmed. Readout & Thermal Benefits: Faster logic circuitry can help speed up sensor readout, multi-frame capture, and high-frame-rate or HDR video while cutting heat and power draw. Samsung Austin & 17nm LPV Context: Industry reporting notes Samsung’s 17nm Low Power Value (17LPV) image-sensor logic process and Apple-Samsung sensor work in Austin, Texas, though official specs are still unannounced.

Rather than focusing on headline megapixel numbers, the latest leak around the rumored iPhone 20 Pro centers on the 17-nanometer logic process driving the main camera sensor’s readout and signal-processing circuitry. Shrinking the logic layer that converts and transfers pixel data lets the sensor move information faster without forcing the physical light-capturing area itself to grow.

In practical camera terms, a more capable sensor logic layer can support several behind-the-scenes improvements:

While a faster logic layer alone does not guarantee larger light-gathering pixels, it gives Apple’s image signal processor and computational pipeline higher-speed data throughput to work with.

Alongside the 17nm logic rumor, earlier reporting has pointed toward a three-layer stacked sensor design for next-generation camera hardware. Unlike conventional two-layer stacked sensors, a three-layer architecture separates light-collecting photodiodes from dedicated signal-processing and memory/logic layers to reduce electrical interference and boost bandwidth.

The Hisense U6SF Pro is another example of how quickly display technology previously associated with more expensive televisions is moving into more accessible models. At the heart of the TV is a combination of Hi-QLED and MiniLED technology, backed by Full Array Local Dimming, up to 1,200 nits of peak brightness and a native 144Hz refresh rate.

Hisense has built plenty around that display, including its Hi-View AI Engine, Pantone Validated colour, extensive HDR compatibility and a comprehensive collection of gaming features. Fire TV with Alexa+ handles the smart TV experience, while Dolby Atmos, DTS Virtual:X and a built-in subwoofer provide a more substantial audio specification than you might expect from a slim television.

Available in sizes ranging from 55 inches all the way up to 100 inches, the U6SF Pro is designed to cover everything from everyday streaming and movies to sports and high-refresh-rate gaming. Hisense describes its approach as “Premium Picture Within Reach”, so let’s take a closer look at what the U6SF Pro offers.

Picture quality is naturally the main attraction, with Hisense combining Hi-QLED colour with MiniLED backlighting. The smaller LEDs used by MiniLED allow the television to control illumination across the display more precisely than a conventional LED backlight.

The U6SF Pro combines this with Full Array Local Dimming, offering up to 600+ local dimming zones depending on screen size. Individual areas of the backlight can therefore be adjusted according to what is happening on screen, allowing bright highlights to remain bright while reducing illumination behind darker portions of an image.

Peak brightness reaches up to 1,200 nits, although Hisense notes that both peak brightness and the number of local dimming zones vary depending on screen size. Together, the MiniLED backlight, local dimming and high peak brightness give the U6SF Pro a strong foundation for HDR movies, television and games.

Hi-QLED handles colour reproduction, while Pantone Validated colour is another welcome addition. Hisense is aiming for vivid but natural-looking colours across everything from cinematic skin tones to sports, landscapes and detailed gaming environments.

Brightness is only part of the equation when a television is being used in a well-lit room. Reflections from windows and lighting can quickly become distracting, particularly with larger screens, so Hisense has focused on reducing distracting reflections on the U6SF Pro with its anti-reflection technology.

Combined with brightness of up to 1,200 nits, this should make the television particularly useful for daytime viewing and sports. The benefit becomes increasingly relevant as screen size increases, and Hisense specifically lists the 100-inch U6SF Pro as featuring a Glare Free Screen.

This is a practical feature that could make a significant difference depending on where the TV is installed. Not everyone watches movies in a darkened room, and a television designed to cope with more challenging lighting conditions should be considerably more versatile.

The Hisense U6SF Pro’s native 144Hz refresh rate is particularly notable at this point in Hisense’s range. A high refresh rate isn’t only useful for gaming; it can also benefit fast-moving sports and action, where keeping rapid movement clear and easy to follow is important.

Hisense combines the native 144Hz panel with AI Smooth Motion and Motion Rate 480 to improve the presentation of fast-moving content. For gaming, the specification becomes even more interesting, with two HDMI 2.1 ports capable of handling 4K at up to 144Hz.

AMD FreeSync Premium Pro is included alongside Dolby Vision Gaming and HDR10+ Gaming. FreeSync allows the television’s refresh rate to synchronise more closely with the frame rate produced by compatible gaming hardware, helping to reduce screen tearing and provide smoother gameplay.

This gives the U6SF Pro a strong specification for owners of modern consoles and gaming PCs. The 100-inch model differs slightly from the rest of the range, with Hisense listing AMD FreeSync Premium rather than FreeSync Premium Pro.

Hisense has included an impressively comprehensive selection of HDR formats. The U6SF Pro supports Dolby Vision, Dolby Vision IQ, HDR10, HDR10+, HDR10+ Adaptive and HLG, meaning buyers aren’t tied to a particular HDR ecosystem.

Dolby Vision IQ and HDR10+ Adaptive can take viewing conditions into account when presenting compatible HDR content, which should prove useful as lighting changes throughout the day. Filmmaker Mode is also available for viewers looking for a presentation closer to the filmmaker’s original creative intent, while IMAX Enhanced certification provides another option for compatible movies and content.

The U6SF Pro also features Hisense’s Hi-View AI Engine, which automatically adjusts the picture according to the content being displayed. Movies, sports, and games can have very different picture requirements, and the processing system is designed to adapt accordingly rather than requiring the viewer to continually change settings. The AI processing also helps upscale lower-resolution content towards 4K, improving clarity and detail when watching sources that aren’t available in native 4K.

It’s an increasingly important part of the modern TV experience. The physical capabilities of the MiniLED panel provide the foundation, while intelligent processing helps make the most of that hardware across different sources and types of content.

Fire TV provides the smart TV platform on the U6SF Pro, bringing streaming services, apps and content recommendations together within a familiar interface. The latest interface includes dedicated content categories and lets users pin favourite apps for quicker access.

Alexa+ adds voice control through the supplied Alexa Voice Remote. You can use voice commands to find shows, launch apps, adjust the volume, check sports scores and set reminders. Alexa+ can also control compatible smart home devices directly from the television.

It’s a useful combination for a modern TV where finding content has become almost as important as displaying it. Rather than continually moving between individual streaming applications, Fire TV and Alexa+ are designed to make discovering and accessing content considerably simpler.

Sound is another area where Hisense has given the U6SF Pro more than the basics. The television features a 2.1-channel audio system with a built-in subwoofer and up to 50W of output, depending on the model.

The dedicated subwoofer is designed to provide deeper bass for movies, games, sports, and music, while Dolby Atmos and DTS Virtual:X add support for a more immersive sound experience. Bluetooth Audio is supported as well.

A dedicated soundbar or home cinema system will naturally offer more for buyers who want a substantial cinematic audio setup, especially alongside one of the larger U6SF Pro models. However, the inclusion of a built-in subwoofer makes the TV’s integrated audio system a more complete starting point.

There are four HDMI connections on the Hisense U6SF Pro. Two are HDMI 2.1 ports supporting 4K at up to 144Hz, while the remaining two HDMI 2.0 connections support 4K at 60Hz. This gives owners the option of reserving the higher-bandwidth ports for a gaming console or PC while using the remaining connections for other equipment.

You also get two USB ports, comprising USB 3.0 and USB 2.0, along with Ethernet, an RF antenna connection and optical digital audio output. Wi-Fi 6 provides wireless connectivity and is designed to deliver a stable connection for bandwidth-intensive activities such as 4K streaming, cloud gaming and households with multiple connected devices.

Hisense has wrapped everything in what it calls a Unibody Slim Design, with an edge-to-edge display intended to minimise distractions around the picture. This becomes particularly important at larger sizes, where the television inevitably becomes a significant feature of the room.

There is an unusually broad choice of sizes, with the U6SF Pro available in 55-inch, 65-inch, 75-inch, 85-inch and 100-inch versions. That gives buyers options ranging from a conventional living-room television to a genuinely large-screen home entertainment setup.

Hisense backs the U6SF Pro with a two-year warranty, adding some extra reassurance for buyers. That’s particularly welcome on a television incorporating technologies such as MiniLED backlighting, advanced image processing, a high-refresh-rate panel and an integrated smart TV platform.

The warranty also complements the U6SF Pro’s focus on making premium television technology more accessible, providing two years of coverage as part of the overall package. Buyers should, of course, check the applicable warranty terms for their particular model and region.

Black Friday 2026 brings some impressive savings across the Hisense U6SF Pro MiniLED TV range, with discounts of up to 52.5% on selected models. Whether you’re looking for a 55-inch television or a massive 100-inch screen for your home cinema, there are some attractive offers available.

The 85-inch model offers the largest percentage discount, with a saving of $1,050, while the 65-inch version is particularly appealing at just $529.99. For buyers looking for the biggest screen, the 100-inch model offers the largest dollar saving at $1,502.

These promotional prices make the U6SF Pro range even more attractive, bringing MiniLED technology, native 144Hz refresh rates and advanced gaming features to a wider range of budgets.

The Hisense U6SF Pro brings together an impressive collection of technologies. Hi-QLED colour, MiniLED backlighting, Full Array Local Dimming, up to 1,200 nits of peak brightness and a native 144Hz refresh rate provide the foundations, while extensive HDR support, Pantone Validated colour and the Hi-View AI Engine build on them.

It’s also particularly well equipped for gaming. Two 4K/144Hz HDMI connections, AMD FreeSync support, Dolby Vision Gaming and HDR10+ Gaming mean the U6SF Pro should be equally comfortable connected to a modern console or gaming PC as it is streaming a movie or showing a football match.

Fire TV with Alexa+ provides a comprehensive smart TV experience, while the anti-reflection display, Wi-Fi 6, built-in subwoofer and two-year warranty round out an already extensive specification. The choice of 55, 65, 75, 85 and 100-inch models also means there should be a U6SF Pro suitable for a wide variety of rooms.

There are some specification differences between sizes, particularly around peak brightness, local dimming, and the FreeSync implementation on the 100-inch model, so it’s worth checking the specifications of the particular size you’re considering.

Overall, though, the U6SF Pro fits Hisense’s “Premium Picture Within Reach” philosophy particularly well. It combines many of the display, gaming, and smart TV technologies associated with more expensive televisions in a package designed to make them accessible to a wider audience. With Black Friday discounts of up to 52.5% and prices starting at just $469.99, the U6SF Pro becomes an even more attractive option for buyers looking to upgrade their home entertainment setup. For movies, streaming, sports, or gaming, the Hisense U6SF Pro looks like a very well-rounded MiniLED TV.

Keeping files backed up and accessible across devices is easier with a network-attached storage (NAS) device. It stores your files on your network, but it can also run services that manage passwords, back up phone photos, and automate your home. SpaceRex breaks down five uses, including hosting a custom website and running a local DNS server that can block ads and give your services easy-to-remember names. Read on to see how these uses work and what you need to run them on your NAS.

Host a custom website: Claude Code can generate the code, while the NAS runs the site. Django is recommended for its built-in authentication, database and security features. Run a password manager: Bitwarden or the free, self-hosted Vaultwarden can run in Docker. SpaceRex recommends Vaultwarden for getting started but prefers paid Bitwarden for passwords because of its audits. Automate the home: Homebridge connects devices to Apple HomeKit, while Home Assistant supports broader automation. Home Assistant is generally recommended to have its own virtual machine and network interface because of its networking and USB needs. Manage and back up photos: Immich can back up phones and organize photos on a NAS, independently of or alongside cloud services. Synology Photos is a native option for Synology owners. Run a DNS server: A local resolver such as Pi-hole can provide names for NAS services and block ads. A second DNS server is recommended to preserve internet access when the NAS is unavailable.

You can run a custom website on a NAS for tasks such as employee time-card entries or personal life management. Claude Code can generate the site’s code, while the NAS keeps the finished site running and available for backup. You could potentially build the other four uses by asking AI, too.

Django is a recommended foundation for an AI-built site because AI can choose the easiest route to a task without putting security first. Django includes features for database entry, username-and-password authentication, and protection against cross-site scripting. AI can then write database models and other code.

AI can also write security-related components itself, but it can make mistakes. Repeatedly reinventing website components with AI can also cause instability.

You can build a site on a computer and run it on the NAS through Synology Web Station or a Docker Compose build file. Later, you can make code changes on the computer and push them to the server. As your requirements change, you can update the site without waiting for someone else to implement the changes.

Some coding knowledge helps with setup, and deployment can take more work than creating the site from reusable templates. Still, setup is attainable for a fairly tech-savvy user. Creating a Django site with reusable templates can take about an hour, depending on the use case. For more complex deployments, an existing fully built-out application can save work on components that have already been developed.

Bitwarden and Vaultwarden let you store passwords on hardware you control. Bitwarden is open source, while Vaultwarden is a simplified fork you can self-host for free. SpaceRex recommends Vaultwarden for getting started but prefers paying for the full Bitwarden version for passwords because of the audits performed on it.

If you lose data because of a mistake involving your hardware, a self-hosted manager retains encryption. It also avoids the risk of a third party accidentally releasing that data, even in encrypted form; LastPass has been hacked twice.

Both options can run in Docker, and you can access them over a VPN or make them public behind a reverse proxy. Restricting access to a local network or VPN reduces exposure to attack.

You need a machine that runs Docker, an email server such as AWS SMTP, and a properly signed SSL certificate. The certificate helps protect the master password against a man-in-the-middle attack when you send it to the service.

Caddy with the Cloudflare extension is a recommended route for obtaining a certificate for this setup. After buying a domain, you can use a DNS challenge to obtain signed certificates without paying for them or opening the service to the internet. A private installation can also use certbot’s automatic renewal with a Cloudflare DNS challenge.

Here are more guides from our previous articles and guides related to NAS uses and management that you may find helpful.

Homebridge brings devices into Apple HomeKit, making products such as UniFi Protect devices, third-party doorbells and smart thermostats accessible through Apple’s home platform. It can run in Docker and has plugins for connecting devices. Both Homebridge and Home Assistant have extensive plugins for a wide range of devices, and integrations may exist even for devices without an API.

Home Assistant is another option if you want automation beyond the Apple ecosystem. Its plugins bring systems together, and its automations can act without a manual request. If Home Assistant cannot automate something, it probably cannot be automated in general.

For example, an automation can turn off PoE power on a UniFi switch for inward-facing cameras when it detects a family member’s phone at home. That guarantees the cameras cannot record while unpowered.

You can run Home Assistant as a Docker container or a virtual machine, with pre-built virtual-machine images available to import. Pretty much everything in Home Assistant can work with standard Docker, though it is probably the only use listed here that is better suited to a virtual machine than a container.

A virtual machine can make sense because of Home Assistant’s networking and USB needs. Networking with Zigbee, Z-Wave and multicast protocols is more complex in Docker, so Home Assistant is generally recommended to have its own virtual machine and network interface.

Immich is a highly extensible, self-hosted photo manager that can back up your phone and display its photos. It supports collections, AI photo detection and sharing with other people while you retain control of the images. You can run it through Docker on a simple NAS.

Immich can host photos instead of relying on Google Cloud or Apple iCloud, and you can expose it to the internet for phone backups. Google Photos and iCloud can make data difficult to extract through ecosystem lock-in, so a user-controlled backup can make leaving easier.

A self-hosted copy can also sit alongside an existing cloud library. Even if iCloud or Google Photos remains your primary repository, keeping a backup on your own hardware is recommended.

For Synology owners, Synology Photos provides a native option that works with a local user account and requires nothing else to be installed. Immich is an option for running photo management on other NAS hardware.

A DNS server can connect the other NAS services under names, so you do not need to remember their IP addresses and ports. Pretty much any NAS can run a DNS resolver. Your router can direct network devices to the NAS for address lookups, and locally cached DNS queries can make later queries faster and speed up internet traffic.

BIND is a built-in DNS server, while Pi-hole is an ad-blocking DNS server that you can deploy on a NAS. A local resolver can also hold records for services such as Home Assistant.

A reverse proxy can use those names to send requests to the right container, such as Home Assistant or Bitwarden, without requiring you to remember each service’s address and port. You can choose any available domain name when getting started, and domains are inexpensive. You can also use a domain you own to obtain signed SSL certificates, including when the services are not publicly accessible.

If your NAS is the primary resolver, a second DNS server is recommended. A NAS update or an error can otherwise interrupt internet access when DNS goes down. A Raspberry Pi can run that second server.

These uses require a NAS that can run the relevant app, Docker container or virtual machine; Docker on a Windows NAS runs in a Linux virtual machine. Home Assistant may need its own network interface and virtual machine because of its networking requirements. Bitwarden and Vaultwarden also need an email server and a signed SSL certificate, while a primary NAS-based DNS server needs a second resolver to avoid an outage when the NAS is unavailable.

If you want more screen space without carrying a laptop, the INAIR 2 Pro Go Pack offers AR glasses with a small computer and folding keyboard. As reported by Tech Court, it can arrange up to six virtual windows around you, but you have to turn your head to see them and the computer’s fan can be distracting. The setup is portable, while its estimated battery life is around four hours and the full pack costs $999. Discover what it can do for work and entertainment, as well as why it falls short of replacing a laptop.

The $999 INAIR 2 Pro Go Pack combines AR glasses, a computer called the INAIR Pod and a folding keyboard into a self-contained workspace. INAIR advertises a virtual screen up to 135 inches, though its apparent size depends on viewing distance and image placement. The Pod anchors up to six virtual windows around the user, but its narrow field of view requires head movement to see them all. The Pod’s cooling fan became noticeably loud at times during testing, particularly while reading or browsing. INAIR estimates that the Pod’s 5,000 mAh battery lasts around four hours on a full charge.

The INAIR 2 Pro Go Pack combines AR glasses with a small computer called the INAIR Pod and a keyboard that folds into the carrying case. Unlike most AR glasses, which rely on a connected phone or laptop to run apps and act as a display, the Go Pack offers a self-contained workspace.

The package also includes a Wakey wireless adapter and a charging hub. The case holds the components together, although carrying the full setup is more involved than carrying the glasses alone.

INAIR advertises a virtual screen of up to 135 inches for the INAIR 2 Pro, giving you a large personal display in relatively small glasses. Its apparent size depends on viewing distance and image placement, though, and it will not feel like sitting in front of a giant TV.

The frame is thicker than regular sunglasses and has adjustable arms and interchangeable nose pads. Fit matters: if you wear the glasses too high or low, part of the image can be cut off.

A touch control on the frame adjusts electrochromic dimming without a separate light shield. Darker lenses make the display easier to see in bright surroundings, while a more transparent setting lets you stay more aware of what is around you.

INAIR’s Pod can arrange up to six windows around you, using three degrees of freedom tracking to keep them anchored as you look around. The field of view is too narrow to show all six at once, so you have to turn your head to see them.

Android apps run on a Qualcomm eight-core processor, with 8GB of RAM and 128GB of storage. You can open a browser, watch content and arrange windows without connecting a phone or laptop.

To steer a pointer in the virtual space, you hold and move the Pod instead of using a mouse. Its small touchscreen also works as a touchpad, and physical controls provide haptic feedback. In testing, the pointer controls made sense when there was no table, though they took some getting used to.

The included keyboard makes the setup more useful for writing and quick edits than an on-screen keyboard. It folds down for travel, connects over Bluetooth and includes a touchpad, so you do not need a separate mouse.

Unfolded on a table, the keyboard brings the setup closer to a conventional computer, although its compact layout feels different from a full-size laptop keyboard. It can handle tasks such as replying to emails and making quick edits.

For desktop programs or files that are not on the Pod, the Wakey adapter connects to a computer and uses INAIR’s software to stream a Mac or Windows desktop through the Pod. Performance depends on the network, connected computer and software setup. Tech Court would choose a direct connection for work where responsiveness matters.

INAIR 2 Pro works well as a personal entertainment screen, with built-in speakers that mean you do not always need headphones. INAIR also advertises real-time 2D-to-3D conversion, and you can use the glasses as a display for a compatible phone or laptop over USB-C.

The Pod has AI features, but Tech Court would not buy it for those alone. That view could change if AI becomes more deeply tied into the workspace over time.

The Pod’s cooling fan can distract you during quiet activities, although it did not ruin the experience in testing. It became noticeably loud at times and sits close to you when you hold the Pod. Audio may mask it when you watch something, but it stood out during reading or browsing.

Tech Court would want quieter cooling before spending this much. Compared with basic AR glasses, the Pod also adds another device to charge and manage, along with software updates and heat.

INAIR estimates that its 5,000 mAh battery lasts around four hours on a full charge. The charging hub accepts external power for longer sessions.

Tech Court’s advice is to buy the INAIR 2 Pro Go Pack for a carryable, self-contained workspace only if you can accept the extra gear, fan noise and INAIR’s estimated four hours of battery life; skip it as a laptop replacement. Simpler, cheaper options are available for a larger phone display. Before spending $999, write down the apps you need and check that they are supported.

Samsung has not yet confirmed details for its next flagship lineup, yet recent design sketches, accessory molds, Geekbench sightings, and firmware leaks point to a clear visual and hardware split across the Galaxy S27 series ahead of an expected early-2027 launch. While the base Galaxy S27 and S27+ appear set to retain Samsung’s familiar vertical ring layout, the rumored Galaxy S27 Pro and S27 Ultra are tipped to share a raised triple-camera plateau, five color finishes, and exclusive One UI 9.5 animated wallpapers. The video below from Talks Daily Tech breaks down the latest reports.

TL;DR Key Takeaways : Shared Pro & Ultra Camera Plateau: Leaks point to the S27 Pro and S27 Ultra breaking away from the standard models with a raised, three-lens camera island housing individual circular cutouts. Conflicting Dummy Units & Renders: Leaked shells and dummy units vary between oblong camera bars and four-cutout grids, though tipster Ice Universe insists Samsung finalized a three-camera cluster. Five-Color Wallpaper Hints: Firmware leaks surface five color shades—Navy Blue, Light Blue, Burgundy, Light Pink, and Pearl White—paired with ribbon-motif animated wallpapers tailored to the Pro and Ultra tiers. Hardware & Chipset Split: Both upper models are tipped to share a 200MP primary and 50MP ultrawide setup, while the Ultra keeps the 50MP 5x periscope, S Pen, and global Snapdragon 8 Elite Extreme Gen 6 silicon ahead of an early-2027 Unpacked reveal.

For several generations, Samsung’s flagships have been instantly recognizable by individual camera rings sitting flush against the rear glass. According to recent leaked line sketches and accessory molds, Samsung plans to reserve that vertical three-ring look for the entry-level Galaxy S27 and S27+ while giving the Galaxy S27 Pro and S27 Ultra a wider, raised camera island across the upper back.

Inside that housing, recent schematics indicate a three-lens arrangement placing the main and ultrawide cameras in a vertical stack on the left beside a separate telephoto lens, LED flash, and microphone cutout on the right. Rather than being purely cosmetic, moving to a unified plateau serves two practical engineering goals: it frees up internal space for double-stacked logic boards and a larger battery cell, while creating cleaner clearance below the module for native magnetic Qi2 accessories.

While most leaks now agree that Samsung is adopting a rectangular camera plateau on its top two models, the exact lens count and cutout layout have sparked open disagreement among prominent tipsters. Earlier CAD-based shells pointed to an oblong horizontal bar, while dummy units shared by leaker Sonny Dickson showed a rectangular island with four circular cutouts arranged in a two-by-two grid.

Tipster Ice Universe subsequently pushed back against those four-cutout dummies, sharing a line-art schematic of a tighter three-camera cluster and stating that the fourth upper-right lens does not exist on the final hardware. Because dummy units are often produced from early accessory molds before final cosmetic trim is locked in, some discrepancies are expected—yet the back-and-forth shows that rear camera geometry remains one of the most closely scrutinized details ahead of launch.

Physical measurements from early dummy units also point to subtle dimensional tweaks on the Galaxy S27 Ultra. One leaked shell measured roughly 163.76 × 78.25 × 7.97 mm—approximately 0.15mm taller, wider, and thicker than the Galaxy S26 Ultra’s 163.6 × 78.1 × 7.9 mm footprint.

Those fractional increases align with housing a larger 5,700mAh battery, faster 60W wired charging circuitry, a built-in S Pen silo, and internal magnetic alignment rings. At the same time, concentrating the raised camera island on the upper-left corner could make case selection more important for buyers who type with their phone flat on a desk, while rendering older S26 Ultra cases incompatible due to the wider camera cutout.

Firmware leaks extracted from early One UI 9.5 builds have offered additional clues about Samsung’s 2027 visual direction. The leaked wallpaper sets appear in five distinct shades—Navy Blue, Light Blue, Burgundy, Light Pink, and Pearl White—suggesting a coordinated five-color palette across the lineup, though official retail color names have not yet been confirmed.

More notably, the wallpaper assets reinforce the tier separation between standard and upper models. Both the Galaxy S27 Pro and S27 Ultra are tipped to include exclusive animated lock-screen wallpapers featuring a twisted ribbon motif shaped like the letter “S,” adding subtle motion effects tailored to their higher-resolution panels.

Recent benchmark sightings add further context to how Samsung is positioning the four-model family. A Geekbench v7.1 listing tied to the Galaxy S27 Pro surfaced with Samsung’s 2nm Exynos 2700 processor—scoring 3,061 in single-core and 10,967 in multi-core tests—suggesting Samsung will split the S27, S27+, and S27 Pro between Exynos 2700 in global markets and Qualcomm’s Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 6 in regions such as the US and China. By contrast, the Galaxy S27 Ultra is widely expected to ship globally with the higher-binned Snapdragon 8 Elite Extreme Gen 6 alongside 12GB or 16GB of RAM.

On the manufacturing side, South Korean supply-chain reports indicate Samsung is heavily weighting initial output toward its upper tiers, reportedly allocating more than 70% of early S27 production to the Galaxy S27 Ultra (around 18 million units) and Galaxy S27 Pro (7 to 8 million units) ahead of an expected January or February 2027 Galaxy Unpacked reveal.

Despite the steady stream of schematics, benchmark entries, and firmware files, key questions remain unanswered until Samsung makes its official announcement. Longtime Galaxy enthusiasts remain divided over whether moving the Ultra from four rear cameras down to three will deliver the same mid-range zoom crispness as a dedicated 3x optical lens, and rising memory and silicon costs could still push 2027 starting prices higher. Until Samsung takes the stage at Galaxy Unpacked, all design sketches, sensor pairings, and launch dates remain unofficial.

When comparing the Ray-Ban Meta Gen 3 and Gen 2 smart glasses, the differences may not be immediately obvious. However, these subtle distinctions can significantly impact your decision based on your specific needs and preferences. Both models share a strong foundation of features, but the Gen 3 introduces several notable upgrades in design, comfort, and battery performance. Below is a detailed video from GregglesTV to help you determine which model suits your lifestyle best.

More Discreet Aesthetics: Gen 3 shrinks camera and LED indicator openings by 36%, adds optician-adjustable temple tips, and introduces a customizable physical action button. Incremental Battery Boost: Delivers up to 9 hours of mixed battery life per charge (50 hours with the case), edging out Gen 2’s 8-hour and 48-hour ratings. Unchanged 12MP Camera: Both models retain the exact same 12MP ultra-wide sensor with up to 3K 30fps video recording, meaning photo and video quality remains identical. $70 Price Difference: Gen 3 starts at $449 in Wayfarer, Aviator, and Zena frames, while Gen 2 offers strong everyday value starting at $379.

The Ray-Ban Meta Gen 3 takes a step forward in design with a more streamlined and discreet appearance. The camera openings and indicator lights are 36% smaller compared to the Gen 2, making the glasses less conspicuous and closer to traditional eyewear. Additionally, the Gen 3 introduces a dedicated configurable action button, giving you greater physical control over Meta AI shortcuts and quick functions.

Comfort is another area where the Gen 3 excels. It features slimmer temples with adjustable tips that opticians can shape for a secure and comfortable fit, especially during extended all-day wear. While both models maintain Ray-Ban’s iconic styling, the Gen 3 expands its frame lineup to include Wayfarer, Aviator and Zena styles. In contrast, the Gen 2 offers Wayfarer, Headliner, and Skylar styles. If frame variety and tailored fit are key factors for you, the Gen 3 stands out as the superior choice.

Battery life is a critical consideration for wearable technology, and the Gen 3 delivers a modest yet practical boost. It offers up to 9 hours of mixed usage on a single charge, compared to 8 hours for the Gen 2. While a one-hour difference may seem minor on paper, it can be significant for users who wear their smart glasses from morning commutes through evening errands.

When paired with their respective charging cases, the Gen 3 provides up to 50 additional hours of battery life, slightly surpassing the Gen 2’s 48 hours—with both supporting fast charging to 50% in roughly 20 minutes. This improvement, though incremental, ensures that the Gen 3 is better equipped to handle longer days of use without frequent recharging.

Both models are equipped with the exact same 12MP ultra-wide camera system capable of shooting up to 3K Ultra HD video at 30fps, making them equally capable for hands-free POV content creation. The Gen 3, however, upgrades to a six-microphone array, adding one extra mic over the Gen 2 alongside adaptive open-ear speaker volume. While this addition improves wind-noise reduction during outdoor calls and voice commands, the overall difference in everyday audio capture is relatively incremental. For users upgrading strictly for camera resolution, neither model holds a sensor advantage over the other.

Style plays a significant role in the appeal of smart glasses, and the Gen 3 introduces the Aviator and Zena frames alongside the classic Wayfarer design. On the other hand, the Gen 2 features the Headliner and Skylar styles in addition to the Wayfarer. This shift in frame silhouettes gives buyers distinct aesthetic choices depending on face shape and personal taste. Whether you prefer the timeless wire-inspired look of an Aviator or the sculptural curves of the Headliner, each generation offers distinct silhouettes.

For many buyers, price is a deciding factor. The Gen 2 starts at $379, making it the more budget-friendly option—especially since Meta continues to sell it alongside the newer lineup and retailers frequently offer discounts.

In contrast, the Gen 3 starts at $449, reflecting a $70 premium for its incremental upgrades in frame styling, adjustable fit, extra microphone, action button, and battery life. Ultimately, the decision comes down to whether you prioritize upfront savings or the subtle ergonomic refinements of the newer model.

As the newer release, the Gen 3 is positioned to receive longer software support over its lifecycle, though Meta has confirmed that most new Meta AI capabilities—such as turn-by-turn walking directions—also roll out to the Gen 2. While the Gen 2 remains a highly capable smart wearable today, buyers planning to keep a single pair of prescription or everyday frames for several years may appreciate the extra runway of the Gen 3.

If you control a computer from your living room, the Wireless Touchpad Keyboard combines typing and cursor control in one device. It costs $99, compared with about $35 for the Logitech K400 Plus, but delivered faster typing and touchpad sampling in Framework’s own tests. You can also switch between four wireless connections. Framework reports that the rechargeable battery lasts over six months with use a few times a week, although the built-in keyboard cannot be replaced. Find out how the two keyboards compare for everyday use and what you can expect from each.

The $99 Framework Wireless Touchpad Keyboard is designed to replace the roughly $35 Logitech K400 Plus in living rooms. In office tests, staff averaged 73 words per minute on the Framework keyboard versus 61 on the K400 Plus. Framework also averaged 11.22 ms key latency versus 13.21 ms and sampled touchpad movement at about 125 Hz versus 74 Hz. Both keyboards worked across 63 feet indoors. The Logitech went slightly farther overall, though both exceeded a realistic living-room range. Framework supports four wireless connections, one dongle and three Bluetooth channels, and wired USB-C. The K400 Plus uses a USB-A dongle. Framework’s rechargeable battery is replaceable, but its built-in keyboard is not. Estimated battery life ranges from one or two months with hours of daily use to over six months with living-room use a few times a week; Logitech rates the K400 Plus for about 18 months on replaceable AA batteries.

The Framework Wireless Touchpad Keyboard is a $99 keyboard and touchpad built to replace the Logitech K400 Plus in the living room. In Framework’s own comparison, it produced faster typing results, lower key latency and a higher touchpad sampling rate than the roughly $35 K400 Plus.

Despite its thin design, the Framework keyboard was fairly rigid. Its built-in keyboard cannot be replaced. The original K400 was released in 2011, and an estimated number in the millions remain in use, including some dating to that year.

The Framework keyboard was faster in an office typing comparison. Staff using Monkeytype averaged 73 words per minute on it, compared with 61 words per minute on the K400 Plus. Its key feel and full-size spacing made typing easier and more reliable.

Key presses also registered sooner on the Framework keyboard. In a 50-press latency test, it averaged 11.22 milliseconds, while the Logitech averaged 13.21 milliseconds. The test triggered the left Shift key electronically using optocouplers. Each keyboard sent its signal through its dongle to a laptop, which returned results over USB to the control board; the Framework result was considered good for a living room keyboard.

Framework’s touchpad sampled movement at about 125 Hz, close to the internal touchpad on a Framework Laptop 12. The K400 Plus measured about 74 Hz over its USB-A dongle, compared with the roughly 120 Hz considered normal for a laptop touchpad. Both used dongles for this measurement. K400 touchpad performance can also depend on skin texture and hand moisture.

Tech content creator Theo received an early Framework unit and preferred its keys and touchpad to the K400’s. He also found the smaller keyboard easier to hold. Theo uses the K400 in his living room and studio, but not at his work desk. He said the power button on the early Framework unit was slightly too small to flick quickly, but that it had since been changed.

Gain further expertise in Framework Wireless Touchpad Keyboard by checking out these recommendations.

Both keyboards worked across the office at 63 feet. The range test then moved outside for lack of space and continued on San Francisco streets. At the outdoor endpoint, the Framework keyboard still worked but had substantial latency and some dropped signal. The K400 was barely working and dropped off around that point.

The Logitech went slightly farther overall. Both keyboards reached farther than they would realistically need to for living room use.

You can switch between four wireless connections on the Framework keyboard, while the K400 Plus uses its paired USB-A dongle. One Framework channel uses the included dongle. The other three channels use Bluetooth. You can also connect it to a host through its front port with a USB-C cable.

If you use four computers, one Framework keyboard can switch between them; the K400 arrangement requires four keyboards. The Framework model costs more than one K400 Plus, though less than three at the prices in the comparison.

Logitech rates the K400 Plus for about 18 months on its two replaceable AA alkaline batteries. In the power measurement, a Nordic Power Profiler Kit was soldered to the K400’s battery terminal. The keyboard drew about 75 microamps in deep idle, returned to about 1 milliamp after use and entered that deep sleep state roughly 10 seconds later. Its idle draw suggested an estimated multiple years of battery life.

Framework’s keyboard uses a rechargeable single-cell LiPo battery. Its initial idle measurement, taken using a fake battery, was about 2.5 milliamps. Its firmware had not been tuned at the time. It has since been improved.

Those Framework battery-life figures are usage estimates rather than the initial power-test result. The battery might need replacing roughly once every 10 years. You can charge the Framework keyboard from a power source, while the Logitech’s AA batteries must be replaced when depleted.

In the teardown, the thin Framework keyboard was fairly rigid, with an internal steel plate adding support. It also has a steel bracket. The opened K400 was wobbly and used plastic throughout its internal structure, including its membrane and rubber. Its regulatory information is molded into the plastic to save label costs.

Framework’s model uses the Framework Laptop 12 keyboard, with a mechanical scissor-switch structure and rubber domes. The butterfly switch has two plastic pieces intended to improve response and key travel. The K400 uses a membrane and rubber dome sheet without that extra key structure. Its separate touchpad buttons sit on the keyboard matrix, whereas the Framework keyboard’s entire touchpad is clickable; the K400 touchpad buttons route separately to its nRF51 microcontroller.

You can open the Framework keyboard, but its thin construction brings repair tradeoffs. Its two plastic shells use six Torx T5 screws and clips that need care during disassembly. The K400 has six Phillips screws on its back and a seventh hidden beneath a label; its clips proved difficult to open in the teardown.

The Framework keyboard itself is not replaceable: it is melted in place to keep the product thin. Its battery can be replaced using a stretch-release pull tab, and replacement batteries come with adhesive attached. There is no space for another battery protector.

Its separate touchpad module is also melted onto the front; it could theoretically be replaced if the company offers it as a part. Its bracket can be unscrewed, and Framework might sell the touchpad on its Marketplace if volume is sufficient. The K400 touchpad is thought to be non-replaceable because it is glued in.

Inside, the Framework control board has pin-header connections and an FPC connector that can be used to reprogram it for other projects. The control board and battery sit on the bottom shell, and a transfer board combines key-matrix and touchpad data into one FPC. The board is more capable and complex to support the keyboard’s connectivity. Its Nordic nRF54 radio is three generations newer than the K400’s Nordic nRF51; both keyboards operate at 2.4 GHz.

The K400 has a soldered, folded-metal antenna, while the Framework keyboard uses a different antenna type. The K400’s battery connectors are soldered in, and its connectorless membrane matrix is press-fit with a metal bracket.

For a living room setup, the tests favor the Framework Wireless Touchpad Keyboard for typing and touchpad performance, while its connections suit people using more than one computer. Samsung has unveiled the One UI 9.5 beta, initially available for the Galaxy S26 series, with plans to extend the update to other devices in the near future. This latest iteration of Samsung’s user interface introduces a host of features designed to enhance customization, privacy, usability, and performance. Whether you are a tech enthusiast or someone who values simplicity, One UI 9.5 aims to deliver a more refined and user-centric experience.

Native App Lock: Lets you lock individual applications behind biometrics or your primary screen lock while hiding sensitive notification previews and widgets. Dynamic Live Wallpapers: Brings interactive, tilt-responsive motion effects and depth blur directly to your Galaxy lock screen. Overhauled Pro Camera & Zoom Bar: Consolidates key controls onto one screen with a new zoom slider, larger icons, and customizable Pro buttons. Mindful Usage & Health Upgrades: Introduces a 10-second “Pause Before App Launch” prompt alongside a global Medications tracker and Mindful Note journaling in Samsung Health.

One of the standout features of One UI 9.5 is the introduction of dynamic live wallpapers. These animated lock screen visuals respond to your interactions and device tilt with subtle motion and depth blur, creating a more immersive and personalized experience. While the concept may draw inspiration from similar features on other platforms, Samsung has tailored it to seamlessly integrate into its ecosystem alongside expanded lock screen clock customizations and live sports animations in the Now Bar. Every time you unlock your device, these live wallpapers add a touch of vibrancy and individuality to your smartphone.

Privacy remains a top priority in One UI 9.5, with the long-awaited addition of a dedicated native app-locking feature. This functionality allows you to secure specific apps using biometric authentication or your screen lock credentials. Beyond locking direct access, it automatically hides widgets and notification content for these apps, making sure that sensitive information remains protected even when someone else holds your unlocked phone. A centralized menu simplifies the management of locked apps, making it easy to adjust settings and maintain control over your privacy in shared or public environments.

The camera experience in One UI 9.5 has been thoughtfully redesigned to cater to both casual users and photography enthusiasts. A revamped settings menu consolidates key adjustments onto a single screen for simplified navigation, while a new unified zoom bar near the shutter makes framing shots smoother and more accurate. Meanwhile, larger, clearer icons and customizable shortcut buttons in Pro and Pro Video modes make advanced controls far more accessible. Whether you’re capturing spontaneous moments or carefully crafting professional-quality shots, these updates provide greater control and flexibility.

Samsung has introduced subtle yet impactful changes to the control panel in One UI 9.5. A search bar has been added directly to the Quick Settings panel, allowing you to locate and adjust specific toggles and accessibility shortcuts—including dedicated hearing aid volume and audio-routing controls—with ease. This enhancement streamlines navigation, reducing the time and effort required to manage your device’s settings. By focusing on intuitive design, Samsung ensures that even complex configurations are accessible to all users.

In an effort to promote more intentional device use, One UI 9.5 introduces the “Pause Before App Launch” feature. This functionality adds a brief 10-second delay before opening selected apps, encouraging you to reconsider whether you truly need to access them. By fostering mindfulness, this feature helps reduce impulsive scrolling and distractions, supporting healthier digital habits for users seeking better control over their screen time.

Galaxy S26 Ultra users benefit from exclusive privacy enhancements in One UI 9.5. Leveraging hardware-level Privacy Display capabilities, these upgrades protect sensitive views across secret browser modes, private albums, locked notes, and additional privacy settings for locked apps. Together, these features create a comprehensive suite of tools designed to shield your personal data from onlookers in public places. By offering these advanced privacy options, Samsung reinforces its commitment to security and user empowerment.

Biometric authentication has been refined in One UI 9.5 to deliver a smoother and more intuitive experience. The fingerprint registration process has been streamlined with clearer guidance and a cleaner visual animation. Additionally, faster simultaneous fingerprint and facial recognition verification ensures quicker, more reliable authentication across the OS. These improvements strike a balance between convenience and security, making it easier than ever to unlock your device and access sensitive information.

The My Files app has received practical updates in One UI 9.5, adding built-in support for viewing and editing DOCX and PPTX documents alongside streamlined storage cleanup tools. These enhancements make it easier to organize your files, open Office documents without extra software, and free up space on your device. By prioritizing efficiency, Samsung ensures that managing your digital content remains a hassle-free experience.

Samsung Health has been expanded with new features aimed at enhancing both physical and mental wellness tracking. The update introduces Mindful Note—a native journaling space offering both freeform writing and guided reflection prompts—alongside a global Medications tracker for logging prescriptions, vitamins, and adherence reminders. Combined with faster three-day sleep coaching insights, the improved Samsung Health app gives you clearer tools to stay on top of your daily well-being.

Samsung DeX, the feature that transforms your device into a desktop-like interface, receives under-the-hood performance optimizations and improved window snapping and tiling refinements in One UI 9.5. These improvements ensure a more reliable and fluid experience when managing multi-window desktop workflows on an external monitor. Whether you’re multitasking or working on the go, the enhanced responsiveness makes DeX a dependable tool for productivity.

Rolling out now through the Samsung Members app in key markets including the US, UK, Germany, India, Korea, and Poland, the One UI 9.5 beta represents a significant step forward in Samsung’s ongoing efforts to refine its software ecosystem. By focusing on customization, privacy, and usability, this update delivers meaningful enhancements that cater to a wide range of user needs. From dynamic live wallpapers to native App Lock and intuitive camera controls, One UI 9.5 lays a polished foundation ahead of its full stable debut alongside the Galaxy S27 lineup in early 2027.

What do Claude and ChatGPT send over the network? Their coding agents can send conversation history, usage data and other requests, even when telemetry is turned off. Claude Code and Codex help you work with code, but the information they send depends on the requests they make and the settings you use. Conversation history can include files and command output, while extensions and model-directed commands can create separate traffic. Along the way, you’ll see where that information can go and which controls address each route, as Kai explains.

In Chaser’s 2025 study of seven agents, Claude Code sent nearly 1,000 telemetry requests in one run, while Copilot contacted telemetry servers after disabling telemetry. In one recorded Claude Code session, 130 model calls uploaded 21.3 MB, largely because requests resend conversation history. In a test, an agent read a fake secrets file through the terminal in five of six runs, bypassing a file-reading guard. Malicious Claude Code extensions served by Cursor for about 11 hours collected identifying information and attempted to open a persistent tunnel. Apiro found 1,122 public copies of Claude Code’s saved-permissions file containing real secrets, including passwords and AWS keys.

Turning off telemetry does not stop every request an AI coding agent makes. Conversation history, model-directed commands and extensions can all send information through separate routes, each requiring a different control.

AI coding agents work with files, commands and model responses as part of a conversation. That conversation is separate from telemetry, the vendor-generated metrics and error reports that privacy settings often control.

The useful question is who wrote a request: vendor code, the conversation, the model or an extension. Each has a different route out of your machine.

Chaser Systems used a decrypting proxy to examine seven agents: Claude Code, Codex CLI, Gemini CLI, Cursor, GitHub Copilot, Zed and JetBrains Junie. Each worked on the same small codebase and tasks, including reading AWS credentials, across three runs with different telemetry settings.

In the July, September 2025 study, Claude Code sent close to 1,000 telemetry requests in one run, while Copilot continued contacting telemetry servers after its setting was turned off. Cursor had no telemetry toggle, and new accounts had 24 hours to opt out before Cursor began training on their data.

Gemini CLI retried blocked telemetry until attempted traffic was about 150 times what it had originally sent, while Codex sent little. Blocking telemetry servers did not break any of the tools in the versions Chaser tested.

These results are snapshots, not current rankings. The study tracked four Claude Code hosts, while Anthropic’s current list has 18 hosts; Codex now has a StatSig metrics exporter with an analytics setting. Cursor’s privacy page also says requests using your own API key still pass through its back end, where it builds the final prompt.

Advance your skills in AI coding assistants and telemetry by reading more of our detailed content.

Anthropic says Claude Code metrics cover latency, reliability and usage, but not code, prompts or file paths. Its error reports contain internal stack traces, with secrets, paths and email addresses redacted before transmission. The Chaser study’s decoded events mostly contained account, organization, plan, terminal, model and tool IDs.

Claude Code has separate settings for metrics and errors, plus disable non-essential traffic for both. Turning telemetry off also stops feature flags loading. Since version 2.1.319, auto mode with flags off may ask about or deny certain actions because it cannot check the server for guidance.

A separate web fetch pre-flight check sends a URL’s host name to Anthropic for a block-list check, even when Claude Code runs on Bedrock or Vertex, and the non-essential traffic switch does not stop it. Skipping the check requires a separate setting and makes web fetch less safe.

In one code-review session recorded by an engineer in Taiwan, Claude Code sent 29.2 MB and received 771 KB across 235 requests, a 38:1 upload-to-download ratio. The engineer began recording after an alert for more than 800 MB sent to Anthropic in a day.

Telemetry accounted for 7.8 MB of that session’s uploads, against 2.4 MB of telemetry in Chaser’s earlier whole test run; another 21.3 MB came from 130 model calls.

Because the model API has no memory, calls resend the conversation history. In the recorded session, 15.7 MB consisted of the beginning of a previous request sent again. Anthropic’s prompt cache saves compute costs but does not reduce those uploads, and disabling telemetry does not remove code from model requests.

Files an agent reads, commands and their output can enter that history. In one test, an agent prompted to read a fake secrets file used the terminal to read an .env file in five of six runs, bypassing a guard on its file-reading tool because the terminal had no such guard. Keeping secrets out of the project folder addresses that exposure more directly than relying on a file-tool guard.

Claude Code’s web fetch connects from your IP address using the Claude-User user agent, so a site that logs connections can record your IP. It asks permission by default. Developer Patrick McCanna says it can reach destinations accessible to you, including localhost services, router administration and cloud metadata endpoints.

The model can also direct terminal commands, scripts or MCP tools to send information elsewhere. Use a sandbox with an outbound allow list for the task and a firewall for other traffic, rather than relying on an environment variable to govern destinations the model chooses while it works.

Claude Code placed the signed-in account’s email address in model context to prevent invented identities in author tags, commit messages and comments. Although Anthropic instructed the model not to send it to unrelated services, Claude used the address as contact information when fetching Wikipedia data or SEC filings.

A news site tracked seven bug reports between September and November, with requests involving crates.io, Wikipedia, the SEC and the Bureau of Labor Statistics. Most came from background subagents, and the final GitHub issue received more than 1,100 reactions.

Anthropic added a word-matching filter that can refuse commands, writes, web fetches or MCP calls when an email appears beside certain identity terms. Its readme warns that the filter is not a security boundary: an address beside a URL or passed through a variable can get through, as can web search, browser tools and MCP fields such as calendar invites.

A Claude Code engineer said the email would be removed from context in the next release, but a user subsequently reported it was still present in version 2.1.327. You can specify which contact information an agent should use when a site requires it.

On October 29, Cursor’s marketplace served malicious Claude Code extension versions 2.1.312 and 2.1.313 for about 11 hours; Anthropic did not build them. They collected details including usernames, Git email addresses and public IPs, then attempted to add an SSH key and open a persistent tunnel.

The tunnel failed on most machines because activating SSH typically requires administrator rights, and Cursor says uninstalling the extensions might not fully clean them up. Claude Code’s non-essential traffic setting does not stop traffic from malicious extensions; pinning extension versions and checking the home directory’s authorized keys file can help address that risk.

Claude Code saves a command approved with “don’t ask again” as a rule in settings.local.json. If the command contains a password, API key or credential-bearing connection string, the file can carry it into a repository unless you exclude the file. Deleting it later does not remove it from Git history.

Apiro found 14,185 copies of the file on public GitHub, including 1,122 containing real secrets and 1,379 distinct secrets overall. The scan counted 379 database passwords, 43 SSH logins and 23 AWS keys; its best scanning tool flagged 643 files, while two popular tools both missed 215.

Adding the settings file to Git’s ignore file and referring to environment variables instead of pasting passwords into approved commands address that route.

Anthropic retains conversation data for five years on free, Pro, Max and Ultra accounts when the default training setting is on, or 30 days when it is off; Team and Enterprise accounts receive 30 days. Qualified Enterprise accounts with custom agreements can obtain zero retention. Submitting /feedback or /bug sends the full transcript for five-year retention regardless of other settings, while Claude Code also saves sessions as plain text locally for 30 days.
